q: Which method gives back a new array that can be shorter, and keeps the values it lets through unchanged?
why: `filter` leaves out the items that fail the test, and the items that stay are not changed. `map` always gives the same number of items, with new values. `forEach` gives back nothing, and `reduce` gives back one value.

q: What does this print? Type the three numbers with spaces between them.
why: `filter` keeps 30 and 40, so its length is `2`. `reduce` adds all four to get `100`. And `prices` itself never changed, so its length is still `4`.

q: Put the calls of `[10, 20, 30, 40].reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0)` in the right order.
items: The start value `0` becomes the running total
why: What one call returns becomes `sum` in the next call.

q: How many times is the callback called here?
options: `3`: with no start value, the first item becomes the running total
why: With no start value, the first item (10) is the running total. Call 1 already has `sum = 10`, `p = 20` and index 1. The answer is still `100`. Always give a start value.
With no start value, `reduce` uses the first item as the running total, and an empty array has no first item. With a start value, `[].reduce(fn, 0)` returns `0` and never calls `fn`.

q: Which of these change the array you call them on?
why: `push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse` and `fill` change the original. `map`, `filter`, `slice` and `concat` build a new array. To keep the original, copy first or use `toSorted`.
`sort` changes the original array and gives back the same array, not a copy. To keep the original, copy first: `[...a].sort()`.
With no compare function, `sort` compares the items as text, so `"10"` comes before `"9"`. To sort numbers, pass `(a, b) => a - b`.
A function with curly braces gives back `undefined` unless it says `return`. Fix: `n => n * 2`, or add `return`.

q: What does this print? Type the four answers with spaces between them.
why: `find` gives the first item that passes, `12`. `findIndex` gives `-1` when nothing passes. `some` is `true` because 12 is above 10. `every` on an empty array is `true`, because no item fails.

q: `findIndex` gives `-1` when nothing matches. Why is `if (index)` a bad check?
options: `0` is a real position, the first item, and `0` counts as false. `-1` counts as true
why: A match at the first item gives `0`, which looks like "not found" inside an `if`. And `-1` counts as true. Write `if (index !== -1)`.

`reduce` can give back one value of any type, like an object
why: `filter` keeps the same values and only decides which ones stay. The others are right. `reduce` can build a number, a string or an object.

q: What does this print? Type the three numbers it prints for `top`, with spaces between them.
why: With no compare function, `sort` compares text, so the numbers end up as `100, 50, 75, 8, 9`. `reverse` turns that around to `9, 8, 75, 50, 100`, and `slice(0, 3)` takes the first three. It also changed `scores` itself. Fix: `[...scores].sort((a, b) => b - a).slice(0, 3)` gives `100 75 50`.
